utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- [English on French channel] [previous translation continues]... French on channel 4, where I expect English. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Professor Corn, I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony still binds you. Mr. Russo, are you ready to continue cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We left off last time discussing your assessment that a ground assault on Knin was not a viable option, and looking at that in the context of General Gotovina's statement in P461 that he could easily take Knin without any problem. And looking back at your answer, it appears that you did not answer the last question I put to you, which was at transcript page 21335, lines 20 to 22. The question was whether you had any basis for disagreeing with General Gotovina's assessment that Knin could be easily taken without any problem.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer to that is yes, based on the facts and assumptions that I was provided by Defence counsel in the request that led to my -- my addendum, and those facts and assumptions included information about a number of military objectives within the city, statements that the RSK intended to make the defence of Knin a priority effort on their own part, and knowledge on the part of -- or an expectation or anticipation on the part of General Gotovina, that he may have to respond to counter-attack during his own offensive operation and I think all three of those factors would influence his operational and tactical judgement at the time he launched the attack, which is why when I wrote the addendum I made the comment in there or made -- as you note, I made the statement or rendered the opinion that I believed that he would have assumed that a ground assault into Knin was not a viable option, viable in an operational sense in the broader context of the offensive operation that he was launching, the enemy situation he anticipated, and his own resource capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So to be clear, you're saying the portion that I read to you from the presidential transcript where he says -- where he tells President Tudjman that Knin could be easily taken without any problem, you're saying that based on the facts and assumptions provided to you that General Gotovina was wrong when he said that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, maybe I -- maybe I mis-characterised it. I don't know what General Gotovina actually believed at that time or not. As I told you in my original answer, what I -- when I read that in the broader context of the other information I had received, and particularly in the context of the other statements that were made by the general during that meeting, I had the impression - and this is just my impression - that that was a response to a statement by the President that indicated essentially if a counter-attack were launched out of Knin, it would provide a pretext for a bombardment or an artillery assault, I can't recall the precise language. And in response to that the general, who throughout the transcript had been discussing his operational concept of the operation or his general concept of the operation, responds, If I need to take Knin I can do it. Now, I think there are a number of ways you can interpret that statement. I don't know whether General Gotovina at that moment in time believed that was true or not. I assume he believed it was true. And I assume on the night of the battle if he had been directed to make the capture of Knin the priority effort, he would have believed he could have done it. But by the time the battle ensued, it seems relevant clear the capture of Knin was seen as a domino that would fall after he achieved his priority operational effort which he had defined as the breach and destruction in depth or defeat in depth of the enemy tactical forces in their defensive positions. So he may very well have thought that was true, but I guess my point is I don't know -- I didn't interpret that to mean that he thought that was a course of action that he would adopt automatically, particularly in light of the context that led to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, your answer seems to focus on your impression of whether Gotovina believed what he said or didn't believe what he said, but the question I'm asking and maybe I need to put it to you more specifically is: He said he could take Knin easily, without any problem. Assuming that he meant what he said, do you disagree that -- well, would you say he was wrong?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the question asks me to judge whether or not he believes -- what he believed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's not my question. I'm asking you to believe -- well, I'm asking you to assume that he believed what he said.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Then I guess how I would have to answer that is: I don't know what his situational awareness was of the enemy situation at that point in time. So I assume, based on his knowledge, he believed it. He said it to his president, and therefore I -- I mean, I -- this is pure speculation, but I suspect that a corps-commanding general is not going to lie to his command -- his political Commander-in-Chief, his president. But I -- when I wrote my addendum, I'm looking at it from the context of the operational situation that he perceived prior to the attack. So he may very well have believed that at that time. As I say, my impression is it was a -- very candidly, my impression from that exchange was: I'm the operational commander, sir, let me make my plan and defeat the enemy. Don't worry about it. I can do it, whatever I have to do. But I think that that's a far cry from saying: I intend to take Knin, or it is my priority of effort, or it will be my priority of effort. There are many other variables involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could have P46 -- I'm sorry, P482. And if we could go to page 17 in the English. I'm searching for the B/C/S page. The B/C/S would be page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You can see, Professor, where it says "Completed Tasks. "The liberation of Knin, as the main objective of the attack ..." Now, the answers you were just giving me seem to suggest otherwise, that the taking of Knin was not the main objective --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Then what am I misunderstanding about --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're misunderstanding the difference between a strategic objective and an operational and tactical priority of effort and an operational and tactical concept of operations scheme of manoeuvre. The taking of Knin may very well have been the priority of effort, just like in 2003 in Iraq, the taking of Baghdad may very well have been -- I'm sorry, not the priority tactical effort, but may have been the strategic objective defined by the strategic commander. But you cannot take Baghdad before you first secure the Euphrates River bridges. So operational manoeuvre commander takes that strategic objective and translates it into an operational scheme of manoeuvre, that is further translated into tactical tasks to subordinate units. And I've said on several occasions that I suspect that in this planning process, this operational planning process, there was an assessment that if the enemy fixed defensive positions in and around Knin, were penetrated and defeated, then Knin would be like a domino that would fall. And that could very well be the logical, operational, and tactical methodology to achieve this strategic objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, if the objective is to take Knin - and I'm sorry if I'm dumbing this down to a level below the -- your expertise in military matters - but I just want to be clear about what I'm hearing from you. If the objective is to take Knin, you're not suggesting, are you, that that objective should be subordinated to other tactical objectives, are you? In other words, if the objective is to take Knin and you can do that without having to worry about tactical obstacles in the foreground, are you saying that the tactical obstacles in the foreground should, in fact, prevent you from achieving your strategic objective faster?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First off, the document you just brought up to show me does not say "taking Knin is the objective." It says "liberation of Knin as the main objective of the attack ..." Liberation is not the same as taking. In 2003 the United States could have dropped the 82nd Airborne Division into Baghdad. That may have well produced an outcome where Baghdad was taken, but that would not have achieved the strategic objective. Because until you defeat the enemy's capability to respond to your conduct and to dictate the terms of the battle, then that taking doesn't automatically translate into liberation. Now, specifically on your question, what you're asking me about is what I guess I could best characterise as operational art. This is what commanders do with their staffs. They look at the strategic objective, and then they assess what needs to be done militarily, tactically, operationally, to bring about achievement of that objective. Now, I would agree with you whole-heartedly that if General Gotovina had made an assessment that the capture of Knin was feasible, achievable, and that the capture of Knin would produce a general collapse of all enemy resistance in the area, then he might reasonably have made a ground assault on Knin his priority of effort. But I think that when you look at his course of action he reached an alternate conclusion, that the key, the centre of gravity, if you will, the tipping point to liberate Knin was to defeat the enemy defensive forces that the enemy had deployed in fixed defensive positions in and around the city, and once they were defeated he would have the freedom of action to liberate the city. So a commander could make different judgements depending on his assessment of the enemy situation and his own capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I was with you almost up until the last point. The point I was going to make was that we've heard a lot about Knin in fact being the centre of gravity, and if that's the case, in fact, if Knin was the centre of gravity, if it's the hub of the command and control nodes and all the communication nodes, if you physically take the town, then you don't have to worry about cutting off their communications because taking the town does all that for you, doesn't it? It disrupts certainly the communications between the town you've taken and soldiers which may be at a different location attempting to defend the town you've just taken. But your answer said: Defeat the enemy defensive forces that the enemy had deployed in fixed defensive positions in and around the city --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been inarticulate. I mean, I'm referring to the tactical assault that was conducted against fixed enemy defensive positions in the areas outside of Knin. So that was a misstatement. But specifically on your question -- I think you are -- your question is based on an assumption that the enemy tactical combat capability is simply going to stand by idly while you put dismounted infantry in their -- what they may very well recognise as their centre of gravity. Now, you've pointed out some facts in the execution of the operation that reveal certain realities of an offensive operation against fixed enemy defensive positions. For example, you questioned me the other day regarding the use of fixed-wing and rotary-wing air capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I'm sorry, let me -- I just -- I want to keep this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think the question was quite general, and I think that the answer is being given to the question that was being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Russo, we have to find a fair balance between giving an opportunity to the witness to explain himself. And he was explaining that your question was based on a certain assumption, and I think he should finish that. At the same time when I say "to find a fair balance," I think you'll understand that, Mr. Corn, that Mr. Russo must also have an opportunity at some point where he thinks that the answer elaborates on matters which he did not seek to cover in his question, that he has an opportunity to move you in the direction he -- of the question again. So could you briefly finish your answer, and then -- Mr. Russo, then you can continue after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try and be a bit more concise on this point, Your Honour. The point is that I was referring to the 85 per cent allocation for time-sensitive targets for those air assets. That's a reflection of the reality that enemy manoeuvre and counter-attack and reinforcement is a significant concern when you're conducting an offensive operation against enemy defences. So it is certainly possible that General Gotovina may have faced a situation where he could have thought: I can put troops into Knin, I can seize Knin, and then what I'm doing is I'm creating a vulnerability for the enemy to surround those forces, cut them off, and then defeat them in depth. So, again, Mr. Russo, I'm not saying that your hypothetical is -- in the right set of circumstances, produces an outcome that is always yes or always no. In the right set of operational and tactical circumstances, that might be a brilliant tactical decision. But from my review of every -- of the circumstances relating to his planning and execution, I think he reasonably concluded that that was not the effect he needed to achieve in order to liberate Knin, that the effect was to isolate, disrupt, and destroy the enemy defensive capability that had been deployed by enemy commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll try to -- did I understand you well that you are trying at this moment to reconstruct on the basis of the information that was made available to you, to the best of your abilities, to reconstruct what is the most likely option in your view? While you are aware that we do not know exactly in every respect -- at least you do not know exactly in every respect what the situation was; you do not know exactly what General Gotovina knew at the time, what he was aware of; and third, that you do not know exactly what considerations led him to decide on what then became the course of events that we know about. Is that a fair way of understanding -- I would say the type of testimony you are giving at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly right, Your Honour. There are multiple variables. I was asked to render an opinion as to whether the decision to employ his capability as he did was a reasonable course of action based on the facts and assumptions I was given. In my opinion, the decision to forego a ground assault into the city and based on the judgement that the effect you needed to achieve was not to seize the city as a tactical objective but to disrupt enemy capability in the city in the broader scheme of manoeuvre was a reasonable decision by an operational commander. If I -- and I agree, Your Honour, I don't know all the facts, and that's why I say to Mr. Russo if the factual predicates were changed significantly, then it might have been a much more reasonable course of action to actually seize the city with a ground assault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So, Professor, the last part of your answer, clearly your conclusions in your report are based on the assumption that the physical taking of Knin was not the prime objective or the priority of effort. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's clear in the report, that the priority of effort -- and so -- and I think his allocation of indirect fire support bears this out - was the tactical point of attack. He used -- approximately based on the facts and assumptions that I respond to, approximately 80 per cent of his fire-support capability, his organic capability at the tact, in support of the close battle. And that, to me, is an indication of what he viewed as his priority of effort. Because if his priority of effort was taking Knin, I think that the allocation would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at the document on the screen, when I read to you the part about the liberation of Knin, one of your answers was that liberation of Knin as the main objective of the attack, "liberation is not the same as taking." Now, you've never seen this document before, right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So you don't know when General Gotovina wrote this document whether liberation in fact meant taking?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So that's an assumption you're making?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's an assumption -- well, the answer is, yes, it's an assumption. It's an assumption based on the fact that the facts and assumptions that I was provided to base my opinion on indicated that General -- I'm sorry, General Gotovina never viewed the completion of Operation Storm as the end state of his operational and tactical effort, that he understood that there were follow-on missions that had to be conducted. And so it's very possible that he could see the liberation of Knin as the decisive point, if you will, in achieving the broader strategic goal of liberating the entire Croatian national territory, but that doesn't mean it was the decisive point in defeating the enemy defences that had been prepared to thwart that effort in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, General Gotovina's assessment as reflected in the 31 July transcript about how easy it would be to take Knin with a thousand men, first of all, assuming he believed that to be true, couldn't a reasonable inference from that be that General Gotovina did not expect to encounter significant resistance inside the town?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be -- if that is what he believed at the time, then it would be reasonable to infer that he concluded he would not encounter significant -- enough resistance to thwart the efforts of a thousand well-trained infantrymen to achieve that goal if he had made that his objective, but again it pre-supposes that's the effect he desires to achieve. And one other -- I think I have to mention this. I think again, you know, as you get closer to the execution of the operation, another assumption that I was provided was that he -- General Gotovina on the eve of battle was concerned about possible counter-attack by Bosnian Serb forces and potentially even the JNA. So, you know, when you're at that point in time, you have limited reserve capability, a thousand well-trained infantrymen, assuming that they were there and ready, as he anticipated in the meeting with the president, might very well be determined by the commander as a resource that he needed to hold in case this counter-attack materialised as he anticipated. And if he can achieve his effect in support of the ground tactical plan with an economy of force effort, then that might be a reasonable reason not to do that. There are just so many variables in this equation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I try to understand whether I really understood your last answer. Mr. Russo says that if he really intended to take Knin by ground forces, wouldn't that mean that he didn't expect much resistance? That was short his question. Did I understand your answer well to be that: Well, apart from whether you have to consider what resistance you could expect, you would also have to take into account that you may need your troops which -- with not a lot of resistance might be less needed to take Knin, but you might also want to use them elsewhere because you had other concerns at the time? Is that briefly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or not even know where you're going to use them. Hold them in reserve to respond to an enemy counter-attack. And in that regard, Your Honour, I would go back to the discussion the other day about the unpredictability of urban warfare. You can anticipate light resistance, but we know doctrinally that light resistance can turn out to be much more significant than you anticipated. And with a limited reserve capability, that's a serious risk a commander takes when he embarks upon that effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would have to know what to expect, and you would have to have good data, and we do not know exactly -- at least from what I understand, no details were given to you, what was there to be expected as far as troops are concerned. I'm not talking about military objectives, neither were you informed in detail about what General Gotovina believed at the time that he could expect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had the assumptions, and the assumptions indicated that he assumed that there were reserve -- some reserve capabilities in the city, some special forces units, some special police units, and other troops, but I -- the assumptions didn't give me the full ground order of battle of the -- of the Serb forces in Knin, Your Honour, so that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo. I now and then -- since we have complex questions, and we have complex answers, I now and then try to see whether in language, perhaps a bit less complex, whether I have understood what the testimony is. Mr. Russo, I hope you don't mind that I'm verifying now and then because finally it's the Chamber which will have to evaluate this evidence and all the evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in regard to His Honour Judge Orie's questions, do you have any reason to believe that at the time General Gotovina made the statement to his Commander-in-Chief, that he could take the town easily and without any problem, do you have any reason to believe that he was unaware of the factors that you're now suggesting could change the situation?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, it's -- do I have reason to believe? I speculate that the closer you get to actual execution of the operation, the better your situational awareness becomes. So, yeah, I would speculate that he didn't know the full situation he would confront prior to execution at the time he made that statement, but he may very well have; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You made mention in your answer to His Honour Judge Orie's questions about the assumptions provided to you concerning what was in Knin. From the information you were given, can you tell the Trial Chamber how many ARSK troops you believed were inside of Knin on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's what I meant. I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's what the term "order of battle" meant. Order of battle is a term that refers to the actual organisation of enemy forces. So I don't know -- as I recall I wasn't given an assumption that gives me the exact number of forces in the town or in the city, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in assessing the viability of a ground assault on Knin, isn't the number of troops a piece of information you need to know?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this broader context, my opinion is no. When I know that he faces a risk of counter-attack, the unpredictability of what forces are going to create that threat, whether it's just ARSK or it's Bosnian Serb or it's JNA, when I know that there is a doctrinal axiom that basically teaches commanders to beware of urban warfare and when I know that he knows that the enemy has critical C3I assets in that town and their Commander-in-Chief, then I think it is a rational assumption that if I have to do this, it's going to be -- if I can avoid doing this and still achieve my purpose, it's in my best interest operationally. That was the basis of that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I want to be clear what -- what you mean when you say that in the broader context your opinion is that you do not need to know the number of troops in order to assess the viability of an attack on Knin. Are you saying that, for example, it doesn't matter if there were five troops inside the town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, perhaps I do the same as I did before, try to see whether I understood the answer and then see whether your question still remains. I understood your answer to be: You don't have to know how many troops there are if you should not even seriously consider to take the town by ground forces because there are other priorities. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you know the exact enemy order of battle and disposition, that's always better, but if you know that the enemy has critical headquarters, logistics supply points, and movement choke-points in that city, if I were the intelligence officer, I would make an assumption that that's an asset the enemy is going to want to protect. And also in the back of my mind is this emphasis that this mission needs to be accomplished professionally. Once you place infantry into urban terrain, if you encounter something you didn't anticipate, what happens when they need close air support? What happens when they need indirect fire support? Now your ability to control how and where you're going to use those assets becomes much less predictable than pre-planned targeting. So I think all of those. So, Your Honour, I don't think -- I don't want to suggest you don't need to know anything. But my suggestion is because you know there are high-value targets in there, it creates an inference that this is not going to be just three or four reserve forces that are going to throw down their arms on the approach of enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So part of your answer included an assumption that in view of the targets that were there, that you would assume, more or less automatically, that there would be -- well, substantial troops available or to, as you said, protect these targets, and that you have to take into account also that they would be protected by other means than ground troops, and that you would have to consider all that apart from all your concerns about employment of your own troops elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the enemy's ability to move troops to reinforce that asset as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in order to make the determination about whether you're going to use artillery on the town, relevant to that consideration, obviously, for you was the consideration of the viability of a ground assault as an option, because you mentioned that in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated in my report that in my opinion, based on the situation he confronted, he didn't think a ground assault was viable. If you are asking me do I think use of artillery is per se improper if a ground assault was viable, I don't think I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. I asked you in order to make the determination about whether to use artillery in the town -- I should say in order to make the determination about whether the use of artillery in the town is reasonable, in other words, the selection of artillery as the way to conduct the attack, in order to determine whether or not that was a reasonable decision to make, one of the alternatives you have to consider, the alternative of using a ground assault?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a commander employs a method or means of warfare and he knows that that method and means of warfare has a risk of inflicting collateral damage or incidental injury, he bears an obligation to consider whether there are alternate viable means that will achieve the same effect with no -- with no compromise of his effort, his capability, et cetera, et cetera. So, yes, I think if a commander if he thought that an enemy command post is in a location, there are civilians in the area, and he could take it, and there was no uncertainty, it was -- you know, you think of an extreme, like the enemy declares the area an open area, I don't -- I'm trying to think of the hypothetical because there's so much uncertainty involved in a tactical assault into an urban area. But if you could establish that the commander said, I knew I could take that with virtually no losses, and the enemy wouldn't resist, and there wouldn't be close combat in the urban area, and I wouldn't have to worry about calling close air support for my forces engaged, and I wouldn't have to worry about calling fire support for my forces engaged in this urban area -- in other words, I knew for sure that I could do this without the need to resort to indirect fires or destructive means that might threaten the civilian population, then, yes, that would be an alternative I think he would be compelled to consider. But there are -- I mean, I think you can tell from my answer, I think there is so much uncertainty with a ground assault into an urban area that that -- reaching that point of parity between the two methods to achieve the same effect is extremely difficulty, I think, as an anticipatory matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that would achieve that parity and one of the things that would alleviate the uncertainty of urban combat would be if there are no enemy troops in the town to actually fight with, right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the enemy has manoeuvre capability. Listen, if I'm the enemy and I anticipate that your main effort is going to be outside of the city, then in my intelligence estimate, driven by my intelligence, I prepare for that. If suddenly I realise that I've been duped, that your main effort is focused somewhere else, I either have to concede the objective you're seeking, or I have to re-disposition my forces through fires and manoeuvres to respond to your threat. So I mean even if he knew there was a limited ground defence capability in the city, that didn't mean ipso facto he would have to assume the enemy was incapable of defending the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, the -- this is what I'm attempting to demonstrate about the way you're answering my questions, Professor. I asked you to assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, and I would just object to the form of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, would you re-start the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it's a bit difficult for me to get the witness to understand my question when he doesn't understand what I'm attempting to point out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't get that impression yet, but let's just look at your -- you can ask the witness to focus his answers on your questions, but demonstrating to the witness the way in which he's answering the question, that is what you announced you would do, is not the best way to proceed. I -- perhaps you put your next question to the witness. I'll keep a close eye on it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I asked you to assume that there were no troops in the town to fight. Your answer moved into a suggestion that troops would or could enter the town to fight and then that would be a reason not to consider the ground assault. Unless I'm mistaken, I thought your answer was suggesting that even if there were no troops in Knin to defend the town, that General Gotovina couldn't count on that because there's the possibility that troops might turn around and run back into the city to start defending it. Is that --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if the absence -- you said one thing that would create that parity for certain is if there were no troops in the town. And my response was I don't think that automatically produces that parity because there are other -- this is METT-T-C. And, Mr. Russo, I'm not trying to be he evasive. I'm just -- I have to think of this the way I've been taught to think. This is METT-T-C. He has to consider first, what is the mission he needs to achieve? What is the enemy situation? You've given me one aspect of enemy disposition, an absence of a robust or effective ground defensive capability in the city, but that's not the entire enemy disposition. Enemy disposition includes other troops in the area, troops that can potentially reinforce, troops that can threaten his flanks in order to relieve pressure on the city. And it includes the potential that once he puts troops into that city, he's putting them in a potentially vulnerable situation where they can be surrounded. So the question was, Does it create parity? I think I said this previously. If you give me an assumption that says the town is undefended, meaningfully, right, there might be some straggler troops there or in a -- combat ineffective forces, the town is undefended, the enemy is not capable of manoeuvring reinforcements to defend the town, the enemy is not capable of manoeuvring to counter-attack, and the enemy is not capable of manoeuvring to threaten other areas of his effort, the friendly effort, to relieve pressure on that town, then once you put all that together you would say it's essentially, you know, a piece of low-hanging fruit that can just be plucked and why not take it. So in that regard, if you add all those other assumptions, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, again, I'm not schooled in the same use of military terminology as you are, but when you say the town is meaningfully undefended from within, that's one piece of information. The remainder of the things you mentioned, that the enemy is not capable of manoeuvring reinforcements to defend the town. I take it, you know, absent every troop, every soldier's legs being cut off, everybody is capable of moving in a direction to attempt to defend the town. The real question there is what their capability is of getting from where they are to where your troops are going to be positioned in a meaningful way to actually put up a fight; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in terms of --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And by the way, that there may be situations where you might want to use that as bait to get them to get out and manoeuvre, that could be another variable, where you hope that they respond because then they'll put themselves in a more vulnerable position for your attack. I mean, there are just so many elements involved in this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The other considerations that you mentioned all deal with the capability of the enemy to counter-attack or to essentially put pressure on the forces that you've -- are attempting to put into the town you're trying to take; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With one qualifier, the anticipated capability. This is -- you're trying to predict in order to determine whether this is a viable alternate method of achieving your effect of disabling, for example, enemy command and control and communications, you have to make an assessment. So it's not the actual capability. For example, the -- in fact, the JNA may never have had the slightest intent to intervene in this fight, but what's important, in my view, is what the general -- General Gotovina anticipated or reasonably believed might be that threat. So I think that -- with that qualifier, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And General Gotovina's anticipation or reasonable assessment in that regard has to be based on his intelligence that he receives, but also has to be based on an honest effort to collect that intelligence; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, plus one more. Okay. The one more is, this was -- this is what tactical intelligence is. It's putting yourself in the head of your enemy and trying to anticipate how he would respond to your course of action. So part of this predictive process is knowing the enemy's, kind of, doctrinal view of a battle, what's important, what he would defend, and that influences your assessment of what you can expect if you conduct any attack, any military operation. So there's a -- there's kind of a chess game element to it, if you will, and that's the intelligence component. It's not just gathering information, it's using that information, and information is not intelligence. Intelligence is the analysis of information combined with other elements of your knowledge of your enemy, what he's going to do, what's important, his past practices, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in answering question 12 in your expert report, this is at page 21, this is regarding whether a commander should attempt to avoid fighting in a built-up area or FIBUA, as you call it. You state: "If alternatives to ground assault are viable, a commander would be derelict in not considering and ultimately employing them. For example, a commander may choose to use indirect fire assets to disrupt enemy forces in a built-up area during bypass operations or to fix them in an area so that they cannot endanger friendly forces during the bypass." Now, Professor, if General Gotovina's objective and his intent was to take physical control of the town of Knin, not to bypass it, then absent an anticipated or orchestrated withdrawal of the enemy troops that he believes are in the city, one way or another he's going to have to FIBUA them to get them out of the town; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying that using artillery is the way he should anticipate getting them out of the town?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- you know, I'll give you a historical example --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: How about instead of a historical example --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I'll give you this example --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, the question was asked of

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you saying that using artillery is the way he should anticipate getting them out? And then the witness said no, and I believe that he was attempting to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he was going to give a historical example. If Mr. Russo would prefer to have it explained without examples, he can ask that. Whether that's very wise, Mr. Russo, is another matter. Sometimes examples are better to be understood, but the witness certainly makes plain his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The strategic objective is the liberation of a city, a capital. Liberation can occur by destroying enemy forces in that capital and physically occupying it, but it also can occur by the forces in that capital, as you say, either withdrawing or capitulating. And, actually, capitulation is the ideal outcome for enemy forces in an urban area. That's why bypass is a preferred tactic. The idea is that you bypass the city so that you can isolate it, and then the enemy forces within the city see the futility of continued resistance and capitulate. The civilian population gets protected -- gets greater protection because you don't have to engage in an urban battle, and you achieve your strategic goal. The historical example, I mean, there are many of them, but -- and that's exactly what General Eisenhower intended to do with Paris in 1944 in August; he did not want to go into the city and fight. And in many ways the allies were quite fortunate in the outcome because there as a German general who chose to capitulate when he didn't necessarily have to. But General Eisenhower's preference was, I'll bypass it, and ultimately it will capitulate. He definitely wanted to liberate Paris; there's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you're aware that General Gotovina's subordinate units, the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigade were ordered to take the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were ordered to occupy the town of Knin after the first day of battle based on the assumptions and facts I was given. In the morning of the second day, they entered the city from two different directions, but by that time, again based on the facts and assumptions provided, the general was aware that there was a general withdrawal or retreat of Serb forces from Knin. So in a sense, okay, he didn't surround it, forcing a capitulation, he left -- whether he left it at his own choice, or it was just a tactical inevitability, there was an egress route, the enemy availed themselves of it, and he puts troops in to the city. It's a common tactic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, they were ordered to occupy the town at a time when General Gotovina, at least according to the facts you were given, still believed that there were enemy troops in the town. I mean, General Gotovina didn't wait until the enemy troops left and then issue the order to take the town; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the progression of the second day's battle. The enemy forces had been defeated; the enemy was withdrawing, and his forces were in pursuit of a withdrawing enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: According to what you were told, were there enemy troops in Knin on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were enemy troops that had withdrawn towards Knin. I think that was in the assumption or one of the facts. But as I recall -- I mean, I could refer back to it, by 10.00 on the morning of the second day of battle, the enemy's will had been broken, essentially, his capability had been defeated, and there was a general withdrawal, and the two brigades of the professional brigades under the general's command were ordered to enter the city. I don't recall specifically if there was -- I'll say this: My assumption writing it was by that point the general did not anticipate significant urban warfare in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, based on the facts and assumptions provided to you, there's no information about when General Gotovina gave the order to his troops to occupy the town relative to a withdrawal of troops from the town itself, so I'm trying to understand what you were thinking when you assessed the reasonableness of the shelling that occurred on the 5th of August. How many troops did --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can answer that. The assumptions indicated that after the first night's tactical success, the enemy or General Gotovina was aware that the enemy command had ordered a shortening of the lines, which is a common practice when you're conducting a defence, you move from your initial defensive positions to your secondary defensive positions, and that the -- there was another -- the surge of artillery occurred, again at the point in time in the morning that was synchronised with the Croat forces launching the second day's offensive against the secondary defensive positions, which collapsed much more rapidly than the general -- or that the Croats anticipated. But the use of artillery on that second morning, according to my opinion, was consistent with the synchronised use of the artillery the first morning, which is a synchronised effort to disrupt the enemy's ability to manage and see the battle-field when the general's forces are launching their main effort against the secondary defensive positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I try to understand whether there's some mal-communication. I got the impression, Mr. Russo, but please correct me if I'm wrong, that you wanted to know what was known to General Gotovina when he started on the 5th -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: A bit more specifically, Your Honour. I wanted to know what the witness believes was the case inside the town of Knin on the 5th of August when the shelling began on the morning of the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the second day of the battle; correct? Right. And I think the addendum makes -- I think in the addendum, if I don't make it clear, I apologise - the morning of the 5th the enemy still possessed command, control, communications, intelligence, logistics, and movement routes in the city, the same essential military objectives that existed on the first morning of the battle; and on the second morning, the jump-off time was the same as the first, 5.00 a.m., his -- the general's forces were going into close combat once again against the second-line defences of the Serbs. And there's an artillery barrage that's synchronised to support that effort. That was my assumption on the use of artillery on the second morning of the fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, that's the concern I have, because looking at the facts and assumptions you were provided with, there is no information about what is -- what remains in Knin on the 5th of August. Specifically you were told to assume that the artillery attack on the 5th of August began at 5.20 in the morning. You had also been told to assume that prior to that on the day prior to that and on the night prior to that, the 7th Krajina Corps had been ordered to withdraw and that the command of the ARSK had also been ordered -- relocated from Knin to rear command posts. So 7th Krajina Corps is not there. The commands of the ARSK are ordered to move out of Knin. So at least those two things are not the same as they were on the 4th of August. So, again, there's no specific information, unless you can point me to the facts and assumptions you're talking about, no specific information given to you about what remains in the town of Knin at 5.20 a.m. on the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first off, an order to displace doesn't mean there's nothing there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to focus on -- Mr. Russo would like to know where to find exactly in the facts, assumed facts, given to you where he can find the information you have considered in your previous answer. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in the letter that was sent to me by Defence counsel, Mr. Cronin, signed by Mr. Cronin, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it's the May 19th letter. It's 1D2772 in my materials, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just try to find it. Could we have it on the screen in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's in evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think it's D1642, MFI, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that's 1642 in evidence. Is it still -- MFI --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's D1642, then that is enough to get it on the screen. Okay. That's the May 19th letter, page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be page 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think that what's on the screen, Your Honour, is the -- is my initial report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the letter dated May 19th from Greenberg Traurig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a hard copy in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's under the subheading: Assumed facts regarding the conduct of Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and could you guide us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's at page 36 in e-court, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide us to specific paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, at paragraph 5 there's the assumption or the facts relating to the breach of the initial enemy defensive line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the Dinara mountains, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then at 6 it says: "At 1645 Milan Martic signed an evacuation order for the civilian population from Knin and surrounding municipalities. And HV forces subsequently observed civilian withdrawal. At approximately the same time" - now I'm on paragraph 7 - "General Mrksic issued an order for the withdrawal of the 7th Krajina Corps and the creation of a shorter second line of defence in its rear, a decisive defence of Knin, and the relocation of the ARSK headquarters and ARSK 7th headquarters to a rear location." So my understanding from this is that Knin hadn't been abandoned. It was still to be defended. There was an order for a relocation of headquarters. But an order to displace a headquarters doesn't automatically produce the displacement of the headquarters. It's a complex process; it takes a certain amount of time. As a matter of fact, it's one of the most complicated endeavours that a military command does because of the disruption of operations. So if even with my knowledge that General Gotovina had information indicating that the enemy was trying to withdraw or relocate its C3I capability, that process is ongoing. Now, this is in the afternoon or evening of the 4th, and he's launching his attack on the 5th. I think that it would have been a dangerous assumption on his part that the C3I function in Knin was totally absent when he launches the second day's offensive operations. Again, this is the notion of -- you know, the anticipation that is produced by intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that in paragraph 7 you are interpreting this as making a difference in the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you say is what happened here moved forces or out of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a -- there was a tightening of the defensive perimeter outside of the town, a restoration or a re-establishment of the defensive line, and there was a directive to dis -- to move the command, control, and communications capability to a rear area. But obviously in my opinion, maybe I wasn't clear enough on why I didn't equate that automatically with a commander concluding at 5.00 the next morning that there's no command and control in the town. Their ability to displace is going to be dictated by the battle condition. It's going to be dictated by how many vehicles they have available. It's going to be dictated by how many forces they have available. Have they established a rear CP that can be turned on like that, or is this something that they have to set up? Do you send an advance party to set up the rear CP at night? All of this is happening in hours of darkness, while you're under attack, while you're trying to manage the close fight and re-establish defensive positions. So I think at -- my assumption, and that's what it was, Mr. Russo, was that at 5.00 the next morning the operational commander makes a judgement that there is still a C3I capability, even if it's a residual C3I capability, in those buildings that housed those enemy headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, the issue was whether the factual assumptions on which the witness based his answer earlier, whether they could be found in the facts given to him. Is there still something missing for you, then you could specifically ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I want to be -- I want to go through these one by one because, correct me if I'm wrong, you're interpreting the information you've been given in paragraphs 6 and 7, and then you're making assumptions based on that information -- you're making assumptions about facts which were not provided to you. For example, at approximately the same time as the civilian evacuation is ordered, General Mrksic issues an order for the withdrawal of the ARSK 7th Krajina Corps. Now, you don't know, first of all, whether that order was in fact carried out; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. You don't know how many of the troops in the 7th Krajina Corps remained in the area of Knin; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, it said -- the -- the one I'm reading says the general issued an order for the withdrawal of the ARSK 7th Krajina Corps and the creation of a shorter second line of defence in its rear. A decisive defence of Knin. So I read them collectively. In other words, I understood that to mean General -- excuse me, if I'm mispronouncing it - Mrksic orders his tactical forces to pull back from the defensive positions that have been breached, re-establish a shorter defensive line for the purpose of a decisive defence of Knin. So I -- I did not assume that that meant they were fleeing the area altogether because I couldn't see how that would be consistent with the defence of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, the creation of a shorter second line of defence, first of all, you don't know where that second line of defence was ordered to be created; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can extrapolate from the fact that the friendly forces launched their second day's attack into that second line of defence, that it was somewhere between the first line and Knin. That's -- yes, that's an assumption I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So if in fact that second line of defence and the decisive defence of Knin was in fact set up not between the HV forces and Knin but in fact behind Knin itself and out of the town, then that would change the conclusions that you made based on the information in this paragraph; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, you're asking me to -- a question that's based on an interpretation of that paragraph that is detached from the other facts and assumptions. There was -- here's what I was told: On the second morning there was a deliberate attack against the re-established enemy defensive positions that were manned by forces subordinate to the headquarters that had been established -- long established and well established in Knin up to the night before or the afternoon before. So if they were in -- I'm not -- I'm not sure I understand -- and it -- maybe you could rephrase for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure. You're assuming that the second line of defence, the shorter second line of defence is somewhere between the advancing HV forces and the town of Knin; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm assuming that the second line of defence is an impediment to the HV forces capturing Knin; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, capturing is different than entering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- I have to object. Mr. Russo phrases his question in a certain way, and then you say you do agree and you say something else. And that might not be a -- because that -- Mr. Russo is suggesting to you that -- Mr. Russo is more or less telling you that apparently you assumed that the second line of defence would be between the Croatian forces that are moving forwards and the city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's a fair assumption I made, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand the assumption, Professor, and I'm certainly not faulting you for it. I'm just asking you that if, in fact, that's not the case, if, in fact, that second line of defence was behind Knin, in the hills above the town but behind it, that would change the conclusions that you drew based on your belief that that second line was, as you say, an impediment to the advancing HV forces; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the abstract I would agree with you, with knowing nothing else, right, that the -- that -- and the picture you're painting is that the HV forces have an operational picture, an intelligence picture, that looks like the enemy is in flight and has abandoned the city -- let me just finish the thought. I just want to make it clear that if defeat of the enemy ground tactical capability is the priority of effort, I would not automatically conclude that just because they set up a defensive position not necessarily on one side of the city but on another, that that would radically change the assessment. It would depend on the task that was given to the Croatian ground tactical forces that were in pursuit of that enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, the decisive defence of Knin, what exactly did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I understood that to mean was that the military commander was telling his forces: You've suffered a tactical setback. Pull back, re-establish your defensive positions, because we're going to continue to fight to deprive the Croat forces of an ability to get into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And again, your assumption of that is based on the idea that the ARSK forces are standing between the advancing HV forces and the town of Knin; right? Not that they're outside of the town, behind it, defending in some other fashion; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assumption is that that's what General Gotovina reasonably would have perceived that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, the relocation of the ARSK HQ and the ARSK 7th Corps headquarters, the relocation of those two outside of Knin to a rear location, you indicate that just because that was ordered doesn't necessarily mean that General Gotovina could count on the fact that it was followed through. I'm not sure I understood what you were suggesting with that.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first off, in response to your question you said "the relocation." This doesn't -- didn't give me a fact that there was a relocation. This gave me a fact that there was an order for relocation. And my point is that -- again, I'll just -- well, my point is that I think that a reasonable commander in General Gotovina's situation would have to anticipate that even if that order had been issued at that time, under those circumstances, that the displacement of that command and control capability might not have concluded, it might not have even commenced, or it might have commenced in a very modest series of actions by the enemy. So my only point is -- you are asked me how that influenced my assessment of that morning's barrage, and my point is I did not interpret that to mean that General Gotovina knew or should have known or reasonable would have known that the C3I targets that he was engaging in the first morning had been totally displaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again try to see whether I understand it in every-man's language. A reasonable commander, not having detailed information about whether an order to relocate was executed, could not ignore the possibility that it was not or not entirely execute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with the additional knowledge that that reasonable commander would possess on how difficult a task that is to do in peacetime training, much less in the heat of combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, he would consider everything he knew in assessing if he did not know what was done, he would, of course, in not ignoring the possibility, he would include all his experience in making an assessment of the likelihood of this order already to be executed in whole or in part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to keep matters, of which we are all aware that they are complicated, let's try to keep them relatively simple without losing the gist of what the witness can tell us and what you would like to hear from him. Mr. Russo, please proceed. You have six more minutes until the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, does it work the other way around, Professor? You say if General Gotovina becomes aware of an order to relocate the ARSK HQ, he can't rely 100 per cent on the fact that that order was wholly carried out. Does it work the other way around? If General Gotovina finds out about an order for shortening of the second line of defence or an order for decisive defence of Knin, does he likewise have to anticipate and act on the assumption that those orders have not been fully carried out?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think any time you intercept an enemy's purported order, if you rely on it absolutely with no -- no other information, you're assuming substantial risk. Now, you may be able to get more information and you may not. The order is information. Intelligence is analysed information with an outcome, and intelligence is what drives the commander's decision-making process. So in the hypothetical you give, if he hears that there's an order to withdraw the lines, in the morning or that night, if those tactical commanders on the other side of these purported lines that are withdrawing are not doing reconnaissance to try and assess as best they can whether the facts on the ground corroborate that, then they're assuming risk. Now, their ability to do reconnaissance is dictated by METT-T-C, and if they have no ability to get better information, they might -- the commander might have to act on that. So -- and another factor that would be -- enter this equation is even if the general assumes that this is an actual order, it's not deception, it's not trying to distort his perception of the battle-field, and that it's being executed, he has to consider whether that creates an additional vulnerability to the enemy's C3I capability because they got to move. And movement, it means exposure. So that's another element that would go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is probably a good time in my examination for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we also have an estimate on whether you are -- whether you are proceeding in accordance with what you expected so that we have a better view on how long we'll further hear the testimony of Professor Corn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, to be honest, I'm certainly not proceeding at the pace that I had originally anticipated to proceed. I think I will be in better position at the end of today to take another look at what remains in my examination and give the Court an idea of how much time I'll need on Friday or if I'll need additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you also think about how to finish within the time -- within the original estimate of time you gave. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Russo, I'd like to -- the parties to listen to a small story. I'm a medical doctor. It is weekend. I've got three children. I'm on duty that weekend. The weather is nice, but there usually is a risk of rain in the Netherlands. And my question is now: Should I go to the beach with my children? One would say that's what children like, the weather is nice, et cetera. There a lot of reasons to go. There are, however, also quite some reasons not to go. Obvious, I'm on duty, could I be reached on the beach? What to do with the children, if I have to go to a hospital, perform my duties? This is a situation which requires careful consideration of all the elements. You can go on with that forever. What if my mobile phone is very sensitive for sand, would that be a consideration not to go to the beach when I'm on duty? Yes. But if you would find another mobile phone, less sensitive with sand, would that go in the other direction? It might, but if you would keep this phone -- well, you could still consider to put it in a plastic bag and only open it if you're called, which diminishes the sensitivity for sand. You could do similar things with the children. What if they're half in the water and I miss my call? With this small story I'm trying to explain to the parties - and Professor Corn is listening - that there are situations which are complex, especially complex if you have to make decisions, and that you could finally go in all details. And once you're at the most detailed level, you could easily find another detail because I've been talking about the mobile phone, only about sensitivity for sand and plastic bags, but of course you could invent a lot of other things that could either push in one direction or in the other direction. The Chamber is not assisted by seeking further details into eternity, especially if to some extent the facts of the story are uncertain because it would give an ample opportunity to introduce the specific weather forecast for that day. We do not know exactly, but if the weather forecast not known to the family would be this, what would be the result? What if the overall development of sunshine on the beach in Scheveningen would have slightly changed over the last few years, would that be another element? Of course this Chamber wants to consider all the relevant aspects of the decision-making processes of the accused, the subordinates. At the same time, the Chamber considers that somewhere we have to stop seeking further details where the details, whether at least there's uncertainty about whether these details are already established or could be established. Do you have any questions in relation to this small family story? Do you understand the message, Mr. Russo? But I'm also looking at you, Mr. Corn. And I'm also looking at the Gotovina Defence. Any questions in relation to this small family story, whether it will be a tragedy raining on the beach, the father called to the hospital, or sunshine and no patients that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I understand the point of the Court's story, and I have to be honest, it presents a bit of a problem for the Prosecution's ability to challenge the evidence of the witness. Obviously the original scenario that the Court set up about how many children you have, the fact that you're a doctor, it -- let me just put it bluntly. The witness has been given a set of facts obviously which the Prosecution disputes, and he's reached an opinion based on those facts and assumptions. Now, if that were simply the case, if Professor Corn had showed up here without the supplemental information sheet, indicating that he had considered the laundry list of documents in paragraph 12 which include the critical documents in this case, I would have had about four questions for him on cross-examination. The fact that he now indicates that he's considered the critical documents, although not addressing them specifically, he's now incorporated those into his conclusions, and I have to now challenge all of the evidence or at least most of it, as much as I can, in light of the assumptions that we think he should have considered based on the documentation that he says he reviewed. But if it will not assist the Chamber for me to go through the targets, as was my intention, to change the factual situation or assumptions with respect to each of the alleged military objectives in Knin, if that won't assist the Chamber, then I won't bother with that exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber didn't know that you had that in mind. Most important is for the Chamber to understand the testimony of Professor Corn, where the limits are as to his knowledge of the factual situation. And I think that we have established several times that it often depends on further detailed knowledge about the situation on the ground, about the knowledge of the accused -- the accused had at the time. And what then often happens is that we went to freely further explore what -- on the basis of assumptions what we do not actually know and to see what the consequences of such new elements would be. I'm not saying that you should just ignore the targets. What I'm saying is that there should be put limits to further exploring in depth where apparently the answers to some new assumptions may be clear or not clear or lead to other assumptions, that there should be some limits to that. Because at a certain moment the statistics on how many mobile phones had broken down due to sandy circumstances, not only on beaches but also in deserts and to what extent that would influence the outcome, is not assisting the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in reference to the language of General Gotovina's offensive operation order that we discussed on Tuesday, specifically the language about putting the town of Knin under artillery fire, you stated - and this is at transcript page 21274, lines 11 to 15 - you stated: "I also told the Judge that looking at this document in and of itself, I think that it is inconclusive which interpretation is -- whether one interpretation is so clear that it rules out, as a fair and rational alternative, the other interpretation. I think that -- that you could draw a logical inference that either interpretation is appropriate." I then later asked what your interpretation of the language was based on and all of -- what your interpretation was based on all the interpretation you had. You indicated that your interpretation was that the language was not a directive to engage in an indiscriminate attack against Knin, and you gave several bases for your interpretation. And I'd like to review a few of those. Specifically you gave the following bases. "The information he was provided by the president, the emphasis on professional operations, his background as a professional soldier and non-commissioned officer in one of the most professional organisations in the world." Now, given that you've indicated that the language could reasonably interpreted one way or the other, what matters, you would agree, is how it is, in fact, interpreted by the subordinates who read the order; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my original report I noted a principle of international humanitarian law that I think is an accurate statement of that principle, which is that -- I believe it came from the high command opinion, the high command case, a superior commanding officer can justifiably expect that subordinates will execute his orders, consistent with their obligations under the law. So I -- I don't agree with you that how it was interpreted is the ultimate issue. I believe that it is evidence as to whether or not he intended to engage in an indiscriminate attack. As I noted for the Chamber, the language is not ideal by any means. I think it certainly raises a concern, but you asked my opinion as to what my interpretation of it was, and I gave you my opinion based on other factors that I considered, and I -- if I didn't at that time, I do now candidly and readily acknowledge that ultimately the interpretation of the Chamber of what the significance of that language is as evidence of the defendant's state of mind is the controlling interpretation in this case, not mine. So, no, I don't believe it's how it was interpreted by subordinates. I don't think that is the only or the decisive question that relates to whether or not the defendant is criminally responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have introduced now in your last sentence of your answer that you were dealing with the matter from a point of view of criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not even part of the question. Mr. Russo, you asked: Does this or does that matter? It depends on what you're looking at. If you want to look at whether finally behaviour occurred which was in violation of international humanitarian law, then of course it's very important to know what happened with an order, what did they do, what behaviour we find. If we are trying to establish intent, then of course it might not be the decisive matter. It is a -- in your question you say, This is what matters, depends on what question is before you. If you are talking about operational -- how the operation proceeded, then of course it's very important to know what happened, and that may be contrary to what the person intended to do. So here again you put a question without giving the proper context of what would matter or what would not matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The part of your report that you referred to in your answer, Professor Corn, specifically what you said was that commanders are generally justified in relying on a presumption that subordinates will execute lawful orders in a lawful manner ..." Now, what you indicated, as I read at transcript page 21274, lines 11 to 15, was that looking at the document in and of itself, it could admit of one interpretation which is illegal and one which is legal. Now, given what you said, that commanders are generally justified in relying on a presumption that subordinates will execute lawful orders, what I'm suggesting to you is if the subordinates read the order and they don't read it as you read it and they read it in terms of my interpretation, that it is an unlawful order, then you would agree that it's General Gotovina who's responsible for indicating to them what the proper interpretation of that should be. It's his fault, isn't it, if they interpret it as the illegal order; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the abstract the answer is yes, but I think you would have to look at all the facts and circumstances related to the order and the planning for the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in terms of the bases that you gave for interpreting it as a lawful order, the statements by President Tudjman at the Brioni meeting and General Gotovina's service in the French Foreign Legion, do you have any reason to believe that the subordinates who were reading General Gotovina's offensive operation order had any idea about his service in the French Foreign Legion or the statements made to him at the Brioni meeting?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm at a disadvantage obviously because I don't have the transcript in front of me, but my recollection is fairly clear that those -- if this was one point in time when we discussed it, I'm certain we discussed this issue at other points in time.
