And one of the points I made was you have to look at it in the context of the other language in the order itself, which talks about putting tactical targets under attack. And I remember you and I had an exchange on the fact that I think the preceding paragraph talked about attacking command, control, and communication. And there's another line that says, Put the town of Knin under attack. And we had an exchange as to whether or not the reference to command, control, and communication in the prior paragraph essentially would have been redundant with place -- placing those same targets under attack in Knin. And I told you I didn't think that was necessarily the interpretation because you have C3I capabilities related to the close fight, the tactical fight, and the fight in depth. So I only say this because I think in order to answer your question I have to point out that I think there are other elements related to the interpretation that led to my opinion that there are alternate inferences you could draw from that. If all there was was one line in one order that said put the town of Knin under attack - and, Your Honour, I'm not trying to go down that multiple make-up facts road that your story related to - but I would agree that if there was one line in one order and that's all there was, the fact that these subordinates didn't know his background couldn't influence their interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're actually saying is, Chamber, don't ignore the context which I pointed to and look at whether there's more than just that one line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Russo, I've forgotten one thing. When you earlier said I wanted to go through all the targets, I didn't discourage you to do that. Another way of approaching it is that sometimes matters become clear by way of giving one or two or three examples, or as you would explore one or two or three of these targets. It could be that there would be an understanding of how this expert would look at those facts. Sometimes that sufficiently assists in understanding his views on these kind of matters. So that's an option that's still open. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, given that you placed at least some emphasis on the statements that President Tudjman made to General Gotovina at the Brioni meeting in terms of interpreting General Gotovina's language in the operational order, I'd like to look at some other portions of that meeting and put my interpretations to you and see what you have to say about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please have P461, and if we could go to page 15 in the English and page 28 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm looking at the paragraph that begins with "President" towards the middle, a few sentences into that paragraph it begins: "... but I've said, and we've said it here, that they should be given a way out here ... because it is important that those civilians set out, and then the army will follow them, and when the columns set out, they will have a psychological impact on each other." Professor, didn't you consider this statement by President Tudjman in the presence of General Gotovina to be significant in terms of interpreting the order that General Gotovina gave to put the towns of Knin, Dvar, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that wasn't his statement, his statement follows it, where he notes as a fact that based on the operations that are already ongoing, civilians are leaving, and he anticipates that they're going to continue to leave. So again -- I mean, you're trying to -- you're asking me -- yes, I considered it and I considered it to be another -- I considered it that there was a good probability that it was another exchange that was similar to the other exchange about putting a pretext for attacking Knin and the general's response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you consider the alternate interpretation, that President Tudjman was, in fact, telling all of the military commanders present that it was important as part of the operation to get the Serb civilians out of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, and I -- I mean, I have not studied in depth evidence related to President Tudjman or his conduct during this conflict or his objectives, but I -- I think I said in the -- in relation to the last portion of this transcript we looked at, that in my view you have an operational commander sitting with his president confronting a president who's pushing the envelope, so to speak. And my sense is that the operational commander throughout this transcript is pushing back, basically saying, Let me do my job. Let me fight the enemy and defeat him. So -- I mean, I don't see how you can read the president's statement as anything other than an expression of his belief, that there might be a military advantage that could be exploited as a result of the civilians fleeing the area. Now, even that leads to speculation as to whether that is a reflection of his intent to use civilian terror as a method of warfare, which would be clearly prohibited, or to take advantage of the fact that civilians are fleeing and that might produce a psychological effect on your enemy. But I don't -- I guess my point is, counsel, I didn't read the general's response as an endorsement of using the civilian population as a method of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me first see if I can clarify the first part of your answer. You do agree that one interpretation of President Tudjman's statements is that he did, in fact, want to use the civilian population as a means to affect the military, which you agree would be unlawful; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it would be unlawful if you used military means to force that effect on the civilians. I don't believe it's unlawful to acknowledge that civilians fleeing a conflict area, which is a very common practice, is something that might produce an effect on the enemy forces. Acknowledging that I don't think is unlawful. Making an effort to cause that flight through terrorising the civilian population is clearly unlawful, and I think it could be interpreted either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at General Gotovina's response: "A large number of civilians are already evacuating Knin and heading towards Banja Luka and Belgrade. That means that if we continue this pressure, probably for some time to come, there won't be too many civilians just those who have to stay, who have no possibility of leaving."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it reads "so many civilians" instead of "too many civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apology, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, isn't one interpretation of General Gotovina's response here that he is, in fact, endorsing what President Tudjman says and simply indicating that if they continue to pressure the civilians in the RSK, as they're currently doing, that they will in fact leave, and civilians will not be a concern?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you're assuming that the word "pressure" relates to pressure being imposed on civilians. And I look back at that first exchange he had with the president on using a counter-attack out of Knin as a pretext for attacking Knin, and the general pushes back and says: I got it. I can take care of Knin. I can respond to a counter-attack. I've got it. Here he says "pressure," but he's been talking through this transcript, to the best of my recollection - and I haven't -- I don't have the whole thing in front of me with notes - but as I recall he's been referencing through this transcript his planning, operational focus, his battle focus. So I think in context - and again, this is not my ultimate judgement to make - but I think -- my reaction was in context this indicates that he's saying if we continue the military success we've been having, the military pressure, there's going to be a natural exodus of civilians from the conflict area. So, Mr. President, leave it. Let me do my job. We don't have to worry about making this an objective. And an alternate interpretation is certainly rational. I don't say that mine is correct or incorrect. I just think that you have to interpret it in the broader context of what he was doing to prepare for this fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to the portion of the transcript that you keep making reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could go to page 10 in the English and page 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you just mentioned now, and I believe you also referenced earlier your interpretation of the pretext to strike Knin with artillery, and you believe that General Gotovina's response to that was attempting to dissuade President Tudjman from an overzealous use of artillery in Knin. Is that correct, the way I'm understanding your answer?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- would you restate it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me just be more precise. When I asked you originally about General Gotovina's statement about taking Knin easily with a thousand men you stated - this is at transcript page 21337, lines 8 to 14 - you answered: "It is possible to read this as General Gotovina saying, As part of my plan, I'm ready to just march into Knin. But I think in the broader context, it suggests something quite different, which is he is trying to push the president off this kind of overzealous pressure to put Knin under fire." I quoted you correctly, I know because I looked at the transcript. But is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes. As I said, my interpretation of this, and it's based on the tone, if you will, or the -- I don't know what the right characterisation -- the flavour of General Gotovina's participation in these discussions throughout the transcript, is you have an operational commander dealing with a political leader, national leader, who's straying into his turf. What any operational commander is going to want is for the political leader to set the strategic objective and then let the operational commander plan it and execute it. And so you see -- when I read this, this is what jumped out at me. The president is talking about a counter-attack out of Knin and a pretext for placing it under artillery fire, and the general response by just saying: I've got this situation in hand, I've got it under control. Don't worry about what we're going to have to do with Knin. I'll deal with it within the broader context of my plan. Now, that's my impression. It may be wrong. Others may think it's irrational. But I think in the overall context of his dialogue in this meeting connected - and I don't think you can divorce this - connected with things like the fact that he allocates 80 per cent of his indirect fire to the tactical point of execution in the fight for Knin -- or in the fight to defeat the Serb forces, points -- supports this inference. But all it is, is an inference drawn from circumstantial evidence. Again, Your Honour, I just believe you can't just read it in isolation; I didn't when I rendered my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I want to read the exchange to you and then I'm going to put to you what my interpretation of it was and ask you if you think that's also a reasonable interpretation. Now, beginning -- President Tudjman says: "Gentlemen, I accept your views in principle. There is still something missing" -- sorry, "there is something still missing, and that is the fact that in such a situation when we undertake a general offensive in the entire area, even greater panic will break out in Knin than has to date. Accordingly, we should provide for certain forces which will be directly engaged in the direction of Knin. And, particularly, gentlemen, please remember how many Croatian villages and towns have been destroyed, but that's still not the situation in Knin today ... Therefore, we will have to resolve this with UNCRO, this matter as well, and so forth. But their counter-attack from Knin and so forth, it would provide very good justification for this action, and accordingly, we have the pretext to strike, if we can with artillery, you can ... for complete demoralisation ... not just this ..." Now, before I go on to General Gotovina's response, isn't one reasonable interpretation of this that President Tudjman is suggesting that they can use the excuse of a non-existent counter-attack from Knin to shell Knin?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or an existent one. I mean, when I read this paragraph from the president -- I mean, it didn't look good from my perspective. Of course I think that's a reasonable interpretation of that paragraph, and so of course I'm going to be pretty interested when I see Gotovina as the next declarant to see what the reaction is and then try and place that into context. So yeah, I think that if we were assessing the president's intent, it raises a pretty significant concern, that the president was pressing his military commanders to engage in conduct that they shouldn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's look at General Gotovina's response. "Mr. President, at this moment we completely control Knin with our hardware. That's not a problem, if there is an order to strike at Knin, we will destroy it in its entirety in a few hours. With armoured forces, and medium and long-range missile systems ..." Now, Professor, I'm trying to see how you interpreted this as General Gotovina pushing the president off of an overzealous pressure to put Knin under fire, because my interpretation of this is that General Gotovina is, in fact, the one who's being a bit overzealous and indicating, Okay, you want to shell Knin, we can destroy it in a few hours. And let's look a bit further down the page at President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we can go further down in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Beginning at the bottom the president says: "Generals, officers, although we must not do anything in an ill-conceived manner, we must proceed from the fact that we have achieved such successes, from" --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: "-- from West Slavonia and now in Bosnia, that we have gained the trust of the people, that we have the goodwill of the army, the support of a good part of international public opinion, while the enemy is utterly demoralised. Therefore, we need to be bold. That means not just having things under control, but taking it as quickly as possible, so he gets a taste of it and we pay him back. Therefore, no risky ventures like suffering losses to achieve success. Nevertheless, I think that the political situation is so favourable that we should focus on entering Knin as soon as possible." Now, Professor, isn't a reasonable interpretation of this exchange that, as I said, President Tudjman offers the possibility of putting Knin under fire with the excuse or the pretext that he's justified by what I suggest is a non-existent counter-attack. General Gotovina responds and says: No problem, Mr. President, I'll destroy the town in a few hours if that's what you want. And President Tudjman responds to that and says: Well, let's not doing anything in an ill-conceived manner because, I'm suggesting to you, there is the concern about international public opinion and maintaining the goodwill of the international community. But nevertheless, that the political situation that President Tudjman finds Croatia in is so favourable that it will allow them some room to strike at Knin with artillery and use as an excuse this counter-attack in order to cover up the fact that they're doing it for a different reason. That's my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Object to the form, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think in the present situation, in view of the skills of this witness as an academic, that I would invite him to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, Your Honour, could we go back to the prior page because there was a portion of the exchange that was not highlighted. Towards the bottom. Okay. So I will -- Mr. Russo, I will -- first off, I think that's a reasonable interpretation. I don't dispute that your interpretation is reasonable. I don't think it's the only reasonable interpretation, nor do I think in the broader context it is the interpretation that I agree with. But I don't say it's unreasonable. I think it would be disingenuous to suggest that based on the plain text. What jumped out at me when I read this was when I first started reading the general's response to the pretext statement by the president, I thought to myself: If this is an effect he can have at any time and he's in the position to have it now, why hasn't that effect been executed at least partially? In other words, if he endorses the idea of terrorising, deliberately terrorising the civilian population to gain a tactical advantage by he demoralising the enemy, he's been in position to do that and he hasn't done it. That was one initial reaction, but the first sentence - and I don't know, I don't read Croatian obviously, so I don't know how it translates - but the first sentence seemed -- it concerned me. But then as I read on, he shifts back to his tactical or operational focus, and this is what leads me to conclude that what he's really doing is he's saying to the president: Stop worrying about the stuff you don't need to worry about. I fight the fight for you. You set the objectives. I'll fight the fight. If I have to take Knin, I'll take it. And what was interesting to me was this: I suspect -- and we've spent I think an hour in the last session in a dialogue on this, I suspect he didn't, even at this point, see as an ideal priority of effort a ground assault into Knin, and yet he comes up with this option in response to the shell-Knin proposal of the president quickly. And that's what leads -- I'm starting to read this and saying to myself, and I'm just sharing my thought process with you, what's this -- what's going on in this dialogue? Then the president says: And you should take into consideration the possibility of a helicopter assault. So here we have, once again, a political leader dictating to his commanding general tactics. Right. Now, in the history of modern warfare, this is a common concern of military leaders. I mean, this was the entire -- there are volumes of books written on this in relation to the US experience in Vietnam. President Johnson sitting in the White House with maps picking targets and the utter exasperation that inflicted on the operational commanders. So the president is telling him, This is how we'll do it, we'll shell Knin. He says, Don't worry, if I need to take Knin, I can do it. Here is what I've got. Then the president says, Well, don't forget the helicopter assault. And then he comes back and says, Okay, sir, I'm thinking about that, but we're getting there. And then he lays out his tactical scheme of manoeuvre, which is not a helicopter assault; it's a ground manoeuvre plan. And this kind of -- it's almost like this is happening. Now, what I don't know, and I readily admit it, I don't know the inter-personal dynamic between General Gotovina and President Tudjman. I've never been in a briefing with the president of the United States. I don't know what that's like to be the senior operational commander answering to your political leader and how that dynamic works. If General Gotovina - and I'm almost done, Your Honour - if General Gotovina in the transcript had said: Sir, we don't do that, leave me alone, I'll do this my way, and if you don't like the way I'm doing it, you can relieve me, then that would have been -- I think we would both agree that would have been a great indicator of where this inference tips. I don't know if that was, within that inter-personal dynamic, a way that General Gotovina would have reacted to this. What I'm saying to you is that the reaction seems to me to be pushing back at this intrusion by the president on how to fight, and trying to get the president to stay focused on what we're fighting to achieve, and let me figure out how to fight. But in a way that kind of placates the boss. That was my reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Fair enough, Professor. I'd like to take a look at a couple of other areas of this transcript in order to perhaps bring a bit more context to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could have page 7 in the English, B/C/S page 12. Actually, my apologies. If we could move to page 23 in the English, page 43 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in relation to President Tudjman's earlier statements that we looked at about getting the civilians out, I want to take a look at this exchange where it begins with Dr. Miroslav Tudjman. "Should the information be relayed over the radio as to which routes are open for them to use to pull out?" The president responds: "Yes, that should be said, not the fact that the routes are open, but that it has been noticed that civilians are getting out by using such and such a route." Miroslav Tudjman: "Can we say this at some point at the beginning of the operation? Can we publicise the fact so they know that the civilians are using these routes to withdraw?" President: "Yes, it should be said that they have set out with passenger cars, and so on."

utterances.speaker: DR. MIROSLAV TUDJMAN
utterances.text: "But you will close off certain routes, and tell them which direction to head in, so we have as little to do as possible." Professor, isn't a reasonable inference to be drawn from this that the president in the presence of General Gotovina is directing a plan to show the Serb civilians the way out of Croatia and in order to give themselves less to do in order to accomplish that goal?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I think that the statements by the president in this transcript are schizophrenic in many ways, and that was my reaction when I read it. I was focused primarily on the general's reactions to these statements, because that affected my judgement as to his conduct. And as you note -- I mean, there are ways to interpret this -- rational ways to interpret some of the statements by the president that seemed to be calling on the subordinates to engage in misconduct. But then there are other statements he makes that patently contradict that, like: We can't afford to lose the international goodwill that we have. Now, I was in the army in 1995. I was at the 101st Airborne Division, and we were constantly aware of what was going on in the Balkans during that period, and my view is that by 1995 if you couldn't realise that international goodwill was connected to the way you executed operations, I don't know where you'd been for the last two or three years. So there seems to be schizophrenia in the sense that different messages are being sent throughout this dialogue with the president, but -- but again, General Gotovina's response initially is: They're already leaving. Let me just continue to fight the fight. There's a natural process that will occur here. Now, I don't think that means that that was his endorsement of that objective, even assuming it was an illicit objective or it indicated an illicit objective. He's stating an objective fact, and in many ways in manner that might press back against pushing him into diverting his focus from the operational execution of the mission and the defeat of the enemy armed forces. Again, my interpretation. So, yes, I concede that this could be read in -- rationally in a way that suggests we want the Serbs to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'd like to just challenge, if I could, the assessment you've made that President Tudjman's statements about losing international goodwill are somehow contradicted by what appear to be statements to encourage misconduct. And what I'm suggesting is that what we've read already and the passage that I'm going to read to you now, what they demonstrate is, in fact, President Tudjman is attempting to develop a plan, whereby they can achieve their illicit objective of forcing the Serbs out and at the same time have a good excuse for the international community. And I'd like to read that portion, but I take it there's an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, with all due respect, I mean this is an argument by counsel, and again it goes to form. I mean, he's arguing his position, and heaven knows we'll all have time to do that. So I object to the form as argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the specific context of this cross-examination, the objection is denied. This certainly is not an encouragement to Mr. Russo, and perhaps with witnesses of fact we might have stopped you at an early stage. But under the present circumstances, your interpretation of a text cannot be denied. It may have certain argumentative element in it, but that is to some extent inherent in what is done at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I only have one passage left to read, and I'm going to end with this topic. If we could go to page 29 in the English, and page 55 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Beginning at the top, Gojko Susak: "Third, Mr. President, let me just finish. Can we have your agreement, provided that we will face risks if we lose? I think that it would have a psychological effect on them if we, after the first day of the operation at Benkovac and Obrovac, take the risk of throwing leaflets which could cause losses, but we would know in advance that it is something we have risked, but we could call them on in your name, whatever kind of leaflet we make, after the first day of the operation. We would point out the routes which they could use to pull out, and formulate them in such a manner to double the confusion such as it is. But we must take a risk then and find the people to do it, and I believe that there are those who would take the risk of doing it." President Tudjman responds: "A leaflet of this sort - general chaos, the victory of the Croatian Army supported by the international community and so forth. Serbs, you are already withdrawing, and so forth, and we are appealing to you not to withdraw, we guarantee ... This means giving them a way out, while pretending to guarantee civil rights, et cetera." Now, Professor, again given the interpretation that you've placed on this, that President Tudjman is offering schizophrenic statements, doesn't this, in fact, harmonise those kinds of statements to the extent that he indicates -- my interpretation is that he's indicating showing the Serbs a way out with a leaflet that pretends to guarantee their civil rights. So it does double duty for him. It shows the Serbs the way out of Croatia and it also has an excuse they can use for the international community. What's your response?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that may very well have been what his intent was. But again what jumps out at me here is -- and I remember reading this. How can you not -- how can this not catch your attention? But General Gotovina's not engaged in this dialogue. And again I think that you -- if you're asking me: Do I think based on this transcript it's reasonable to conclude that the president was pushing or pressing subordinate commanders to engage in conduct that could violate IHL, I think that's a reasonable interpretation. But if your asking me: Do I think that this establishes that the subordinate commander, and in particular General Gotovina, embrace that task, I don't think that's what this establishes. And in fact, I think that the -- that his absence from much of this dialogue, that his emphasis at different points in the transcript on his plan to operationally and tactically close with and destroy the enemy forces, suggests that what he's trying to do is preserve his freedom of operational manoeuvre and not get this -- let the president distract him. Now, this is indelibly connected with the facts and assumptions upon which my addendum was written, because if you change those facts and assumptions and you tell me that if the factual record establishes that with a thousand artillery shells there was two -- there were two strikes on a military objective and 900 strikes on civilian objectives, then it would be evidence that would link back to this and any rational person would say that seems to suggest that this did influence his method of executing the operation. But the facts and assumptions that I were provided contradict that conclusion, and that's what puts this into broader context. Not only that, his artillery officer's testimony, the pre-planned targets, the war gaming, the fact that he didn't use his artillery to inflict terror prior to launching the operation, the tactical operation -- so as I say, I think this is a -- I think this raises significant questions about the dynamic of the meeting, the inter-personal relationships, the focus of the general, but I will concede with you that there are elements of this transcript that indicate the president is pushing too hard. I also think that this is not something that's unique in the history of modern warfare. I think that it is -- unfortunately there have been other examples where national political leaders have pressed their military and the military has subtly pushed back or simply avoided that pressure through the method of execution. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, thank you. The last question I had on this: Given that your agreement that President Tudjman's statements can be viewed as pushing an unlawful agenda, couldn't it also be a reasonable inference that, contrary to the interpretation you've suggested, General Gotovina in fact adopted those suggestions and that was the reason that he wrote such a clearly ambiguous - in your interpretation - ambiguous order for attack?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think your question has three embedded assumptions that I question. First off, you assume that that is -- that this proves that the president had an illicit purpose. That may be true, but that's one fact that would have to be established. Secondly, you assume that the general's response to the president or other objective evidence indicates that he adopted that illicit purpose. I think that assumption is far less -- is far more tenuous. Third, I think you ignore the method of execution -- assuming that the facts and assumptions that I based my addendum are -- on are relatively well established in the record, and I'm sure you don't necessarily agree with that. But if you assume all of them, that the president did have an illicit purpose, that the general's reaction in the meeting reflects an endorsement of that illicit purpose, and that the tactical and operational execution of the mission circumstantially corroborates that conclusion, then yes, this transcript would be -- would certainly be damaging. But there's one more point I think -- I'd like to add. You have asked me numerous questions on the idea of doing a ground assault into Knin and some of the risks involved, and I think it was clear that the suggestion was that might have mitigated risk to the civilian population as opposed to using the means that the general ordered to achieve the effect he wanted to achieve. What I wonder is from an operational standpoint, if he is aware that civilians are leaving the conflict area, is that something he should object to? Now, certainly if he's been told to force them to leave through terror attacks, he must object to that. But if he was attacking an area with a civilian population and had made efforts to warn the civilians and encourage them to get out of harm's way, in other contexts he might be applauded for that because that's one of the measures a commander should endeavour to take to minimise the risk to the civilian population. So again, I see an operational commander focused on the tactical battle, civilians are leaving the area, that's a good thing for the purposes of being able to distinguish his enemy from civilians, close with the enemy, and defeat him in depth. And that's why I say I -- your -- I think your question is asking me to attribute motive to the general's comments, and I don't know that -- in my opinion, the motive is not clear from the dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have noticed that Mr. Russo has to wait after your answer quite a while, and that's because the interpreters need some additional time to finish their translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: During one of your answers, Professor, you mentioned that if the factual record established that with a thousand artillery shells, only two struck a military objective, 900 struck civilian objects, that would suggest some evidence that, in fact, the operation was executed unlawfully. So I want to talk now a little bit about the facts you were provided with regarding the effects on the targets. Now, looking at subsection K on page 29 in your addendum, you point out the assumed fact concerning the number of projectiles fired on Knin and its immediate vicinity. I'd like to first -- Professor, it's not clear to me what the immediate vicinity of Knin means here, and I don't know if you know, but I'd like to show you a map and ask you to draw a circle around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 7393. And if we could enlarge the bottom half. There we are -- actually, if we can move up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, if you see the big A --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- just slightly north of that is Knin. Now, are you able, using this map, to indicate what you understood the immediate vicinity of Knin to be?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a 1:600.000 map -- I mean, no, not really. And I didn't do it based on a map, Your Honour. The phrase "immediate vicinity" means the urban-populated areas of the city. It's a generic or general term.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You have seen the aerial photograph of Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can I take your answer to mean that you understood that the 800 to 1100 projectiles were fired into the area encompassed on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's a fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for the record that's Exhibit P62.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, in determining, as you've indicated, whether the use of artillery in Knin was lawful, you obviously do consider it relevant to consider how many projectiles struck the alleged military objectives versus everywhere else they landed; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I don't see where you were provided with any specific information or assumptions in that regard, so I'd like to know what information you used in coming to your conclusions, given that you consider this to be a relevant piece of information.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Well, the -- the assumptions indicate to me the objectives, and my understanding was these were the objectives placed under attack. I think -- so my focus was -- the opinion is probably based on the assumption that the artillery was directed towards those objectives. And I also had in mind, I'm sure, an -- the initial observation report from the UN monitors that -- that detailed their initial observation of the effects of artillery fire. And as I -- I think I mentioned this earlier, I think I was made aware of that in the Tampa meeting, and it had to have been in my mind when I made that conclusion -- or made -- or when I made that assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit P64.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, this is the provisional assessment by the senior UNMO.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is this the document to which you were referring?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus on paragraph 2. Paragraph 2 indicates: "In general shelling was concentrated against military objectives. The damages caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concentrate to the close vicinity of military objectives. Only few (3-5) impacts is observed in other urban areas." Professor, is that the passage that you relied on in this document when considering -- well, when making your assumptions about the damage to the military objectives?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the -- I mean, you used the word "relied on." Is this the passage -- is this the document that had an influence on my assumption, yes. But the assumption was based primarily on the facts that these were the targets placed under attack, and I -- and I had -- as I said, when I wrote the addendum, I didn't have that with me. I did recall it in fairly good detail that there's another paragraph that says it's a preliminary report, that it shouldn't be released. But my -- what I was asked to do in the addendum was to assume that the -- I -- the places or things listed were placed under artillery fire and whether or not they were lawful military objectives. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Other than that assumption and this document here, were you provided with any other information about the actual damage caused by artillery to any of those alleged military objectives?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only other information I think that I had in mind is, as I said, the statement or testimony about, it looked like the whole city was under attack, that we discussed, I think, our first day of -- my first day of testimony. And Colonel Konings, the facts and assumptions related to his report, which indicated a much more scattered effect of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, the document we're looking at here and the facts and assumptions provided to you don't tell you how many projectiles struck the military objectives. You've already indicated that that's certainly a relevant piece of information in making a determination about the lawfulness of the use of artillery --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used -- may I respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used an extreme in the context of the explanation, and I think it's -- it wasn't necessarily connected to this report. I do think it is quite significant that the report indicates that damage caused by shelling to civilian property was generally concentrated around military objectives. So I did not mean to suggest that if a round hits a civilian object in the vicinity of a military objective, that is evidence of per se illegality. And if I did suggest that, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Professor, I wasn't taking that --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- as your suggestion. What I was focusing on was actually the opposite situation. The example, in fact, that you used, the extreme example, as you indicate, two projectiles hitting a military objective while 900 hit somewhere else. My point is that this report, although it does specify damage to civilian areas, it doesn't specify damage to what the drafter believes the military objectives to be. In other words, you can't tell, can you, from looking at this document how many projectiles hit the military objectives; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, no. The answer is no, and he doesn't purport to provide that information. He's not conducting a detailed bomb-crater analysis. I mean, that's fairly obvious from the nature of the report. In my view, it's more of a present-sense impression. It's an immediate reaction to his impression in close proximity to the battle from somebody who has some, I would assume, experience in identifying effects of fires that, as best he can estimate in this preliminary report, the vast majority of effects are concentrated around lawful military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you can't tell from this document whether what the drafter considers to be lawful military objectives are the same as the military objectives you were told were fired at; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, in addition to being asked to assume that 800 to 1100 shells were fired into the Knin and its immediate vicinity throughout the course of the 4th and the 5th of August, you were also asked to assume that the artillery attack between both days lasted approximately a total of 24 hours, and you were also told to assume that there was a total of approximately one hour to 90 minutes of intense shelling during that 24-hour time-period. Now, if -- after that duration, intensity, and amount of shelling -- well, first of all, let me ask you this: Given that duration, intensity, and amount of shelling, do you believe that the weaponry which General Gotovina purports to have used, that's specifically the 130-millimetre cannon and the 122-millimetre multiple-barrel rocket-launchers, do you believe those weapons were capable of striking the alleged military objectives?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is based on whether or not I believed General Gotovina would have anticipated that those weapons were capable of achieving the effect that he determined needed to be achieved. And I guess my point is I don't think that's synonymous with striking the military objective. I mean, if your effect is to disrupt command, control, and communications, for example, and the command, control, and communication is emanating from a building, the headquarters building, right, that building is connected to communications equipment that might be outside the building, might be on top of the building, there are wires, there are antennas, there may be embedded land-lines. I'll slow down. There may be equipment in the vicinity of the objective. As I noted in the addendum, one of your goals may be to disrupt the enemy's ability to restore communications capability. So it's effects-driven targeting, not, Do I put a round through the ceiling of the building and destroy the entire building. And I believe the weapon systems he used were capable of achieving the effect of disrupting C3I, movements, resupply, and muster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I'm looking at the clock. We need another break. Would this be a suitable moment or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, before I ask you a few questions about the last answer you gave, I understand that you may have approached this from a different perspective, but I'd like you, please, if you could, just answer the question before we move on. And that was, Do you believe that the weaponry that General Gotovina purports to have used on the military objectives in Knin, that is, the 130-millimetre cannon and the 122-millimetre multiple-barrel rocket-launchers, do you believe that they were capable of striking the targets identified in your report and addendum?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were capable of striking those targets. I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one correction. I think I -- in the prior session I stated that the document that's on the screen, I don't know what your designation for it is, the UN assessment, I think I said that I didn't have that in Chile when I wrote the addendum. I was mistaken. I did have that in Chile, it was an attachment to the request for the addendum by Defence counsel. So I wanted to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, given that you believe that the weaponry was capable of striking the targets identified in your report and addendum, I'd like you to assume that if after the 24 hours of shelling that you were asked to assume only one projectile struck the ARSK headquarters and that projectile landed in the parking-lot of the building, if that's the case wouldn't -- doesn't that indicate to you that, in fact, that building was not the actual target of the artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your question was -- you asked me: Is the weapon capable of striking the building? Any weapon is capable of striking the building. If you're asking me is the weapon so -- is there such a certainty of precision that if you target the building, you will only strike the building, then I think the answer is no. Tube artillery and -- is not that precise and multiple-launch rockets are generally understood as an area-denial weapon. I think I put that in the addendum. So -- and to answer the question specifically, again it would be contingent on the effect that the commander sought to achieve. I don't want to go down the road of hypotheticals, but it may very well be that the target area was the area of the headquarters because there were things outside the building that the commander sought to influence with that artillery. And I would just go back to Colonel Konings' first page of his report where he recites the doctrine of fire support, and one of the primary purposes is to disrupt enemy command, control, and communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I'm a little surprised because I was under the impression - and please correct me if I'm wrong - that you were asked to determine whether General Gotovina, based on the assumptions provided to you, could have reasonably made a decision, quoting from the addendum question, could have made the decision to use artillery assets against military objectives in Knin. And then you list the military objectives themselves. So if, for example, the military objective of the ARSK HQ, if he's using his artillery assets against the military HQ, are you saying that it was one of your assumptions that he was not actually firing at the building itself?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if the weaponeers, in order to achieve the desired effect, would have sought to place a round on the building or in the parking-lot or in a field next to the building where you might have a communications rig. And the nature of tube artillery because -- again, I am -- I do not purport to be an expert on the capability of artillery. I have a general background on Soviet-era artillery because of my military education from some time ago, but the general effect is that you target an area. And if you want to achieve the effect on the building, you're going to drop rounds on and around the building. Now, one round in an entire barrage being even in the proximity of the building, unless it was -- there was some high-value item or thing at that one spot, would seem to suggest that disabling the command and control capability was not a high priority, if there was only one round in the entire deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I don't see anywhere - and maybe you can point me to it - I don't see anywhere where you were provided with any information about what General Gotovina fired his artillery at other than the buildings and facilities identified in your addendum. In other words, I don't see anything which indicates to you that he fired at the area around the HQ or at a -- something else around the targets themselves. Maybe you can point me to that.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because what I am doing in the addendum is I am assessing whether affecting this place and the function performed in this place is a -- renders the place or the thing a legitimate military objective. So when you say -- when I'm giving the fact or assumption that he targeted the headquarters, I think -- I don't view that as just trying to drop an artillery round on the building. I view it as disabling the function of the headquarters through the use of this capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Then maybe you can be more specific for us with respect to the particular assumptions you made. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what you assumed General Gotovina actually did when he says that he decided to use artillery against the ARSK HQ building, what did you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first off I had to consider the overall pattern of artillery employment and the ratio of artillery support designated for the close battle, the assault on enemy positions, and the -- what the order refers to as the operational depth. In light of the fact -- let me back up. The report that you elicited from Colonel Konings indicated that it is highly unlikely that with this asset, with this employment constraint, that you would have -- you would be able to achieve a destructive effect on a hardened structure. I think that's accurate. If you recall from the first day during my direct testimony, what I questioned was why there was no discussion of a disruptive effect. So my assumption was based on the function of a headquarters, the resource constraint, the effect he wanted to achieve, which was to support the main effort, that what he was trying to do was to disable the ability of that headquarters to see the battle, to respond to the battle, and to direct the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I'm actually trying to get one step further and get from you how exactly you think he did that. In other words, do you think he did that by firing shells at the building itself; and if not, where do you think he was firing the shelling at?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think - and again I have to qualify this because I am not an expert on the technical aspects of the employment of tube artillery - but based on what I've seen in practice, as I've watched my colleagues in practice, I suspect that the headquarters was the designated reference point because it was a known site and that they targeted the headquarters with knowledge that rounds would fall on the building and around the building in order to disrupt communications capability, movement of personnel, in and outside the building, and antennas on the building, outside the building. I think that is the normal way you would employ tube artillery in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So to be clear, when you were asked to assess the reasonableness of General Gotovina using artillery against the ARSK HQ, you assumed that meant he was firing artillery at the building itself and at the area around the building, or firing artillery at the building itself with knowledge that projectiles would also land on areas around the building?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it would be the latter. Now, that doesn't mean that I think that if his staff officer felt that there was a high-value capability outside the building, that they might not have adjusted the intended impact point from the building itself, to the parking-lot, to the field behind the building. I mean, I don't think that would be improper. My assumption is that they probably used the building as the reference point with knowledge that they would affect the parking-lot, the roof, the area outside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in making your assessment of the reasonableness of firing artillery at the ARSK HQ, did you know what was around the building?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew was -- what I knew was that the -- based on the assumption, the object of attack was the building; and based on the preliminary assessment of effects that was attached, that the predominant effects of the fire were on the building. So, I -- no, in these assumptions it did not say, This was what was around the building. I knew the building was in a city, so I think that I probably assumed or presumed that somewhere in proximity of the building there were non-military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to be clear, you weren't provided with any information that what was around the building itself - and I mean right next to the building, on either side of it, or completely around it - you weren't provided with any information that anything around that building was military; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, there were some objectives here that were defined as, I think, a compound, a military compound, I may be wrong, but if you're talking about the ARSK headquarters, that I based it, as I say, on these assumed facts which are there and the assessment and my view of maps and photographs prior to that where I realised that none of these targets were isolated from civilian-populated areas. And I assumed the general knew that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And again, Professor, given your assumption that General Gotovina was using the ARSK HQ as the reference point to fire artillery at, if at the end of the day, the second day, only one projectile had struck the ARSK HQ and that projectile landed in the parking-lot, that would lead you to an inference, wouldn't it, that in fact that HQ was not a target or a primary target or even a true concentrated target of the artillery attack; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If only one round strikes in or near the headquarters in a 48-hour period or a 36-hour period, then I think you would have to infer that that was not a high-priority target for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: What about a 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same -- depending of course on the other employment characteristics. If you tell me that there were three rounds fired in 24 hours and one hits near the headquarters, that changes the equation. If -- my assumption that I was given is that 500 to a thousand rounds are fired in that 24-hour period and only one strikes in or around this headquarters building, then I would infer that the commander made a judgement that that headquarters building was not a priority of effort, or that the effect was achieved with that one round, how -- however he could assess that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to move off of this particular topic just for a while. And I'd like to address the question put to you about good faith, and this is on page 7 of your expert report. You state: "Because operational effects can often support the alternate inference that a commander acted in good faith, even if the assessment of potential consequences was erroneous, prior decisions by the commander should also be considered in the assessment process. In this regard, while not dispositive, a pattern of good-faith decision-making by a commander could undermine the inference that an illicit effect was the result of an illicit motive of criminal state of mind." Now, Professor, I want to make certain that I understand what you were saying here. First, I take it - and I think you've suggested this earlier in your testimony - that the effects of artillery alone, which I take to mean the pattern of damage alone, should not be relied on as the sole indicator of the intent of the commander who orders the attack. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, you use the word "should not." It would -- if you had other information, obviously you would want to put it into broader context, but it can be misleading, I think, is the point in and of itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if that's the case, then likewise concentration of damage in and around objectives cannot be taken as the sole indicator that the attack was, in fact, lawful; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. But I think in either hypothetical or in either example the further on the extreme end of the spectrum the effects become, the greater the probative value they hold. So in your hypothetical you gave me where you say one round hits what's been identified as a high-value target, and this is the extreme hypothetical I gave before, if you could show that 900 other rounds hit civilian population centres while military objectives were ignored, I don't think you would need too much more corroboration of that circumstantial evidence. My point in this passage is that the effects of artillery are -- when you're beyond the two extremes, every single round hits military objective versus every single round hits non-military objective, the further mixed that becomes, the more inconclusive that becomes as a circumstantial indicator of intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. The second point I believe you were making in the quotation that I read was that the prior decisions of a commander, and in particular a pattern of good-faith use of artillery, should be considered to rebut an inference from what might appear on its face to be physical evidence of an unlawful attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I think it's obvious. I mean, it's modus operandi evidence. If you can show a pattern of behaviour, it tends to support one inference or the other, not conclusively, but it's a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And of course you agree that the opposite is true if the evidence indicates that the commander engaged in unlawful shelling or shelling of purely civilian areas in the past, it would support an inference that -- well, let me just put it to you. If General Gotovina had engaged in or his forces had engaged in the shelling of civilian areas in the past, you would take that as evidence to infer that his unlawful -- to infer that the artillery attack on Knin itself was directed at civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there are two issues wrapped up in that, if I may. Assuming we can attribute the prior indiscriminate attack to the commander, that he was responsible for it, then I don't think you -- I don't see how you could ignore that as a factor in assessing the legality of a subsequent attack. I don't think it's dispositive. I mean, I think it's possible you could have a commander who does something improperly, realises he made a mistake, and adjusts his conduct, but it's probative. And the weight, I think, is contingent on the severity of the prior action, how much of an attribution to the commander you can establish, whether it was an isolated incident or a pattern. So it's probative evidence. Now, the other -- the other issue that's wrapped up in that, as I'm sure the Tribunal is aware, is the issue of command responsibility. If it's not attributable to the commander, then the question becomes whether or not he should have known in future actions the subordinates would engage in similar misconduct once he was made aware of the prior misconduct. So I think there are two issues wrapped up with a prior indiscriminate attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you were asked to assume that General Gotovina had not engaged in shelling of Knin prior to Operation Storm, and you indicated in your report that it was a significant factor to you that he had not done so. I'd like you to consider an alternate assumption, that being that forces under General Gotovina's control had shelled a civilian area where there were no military targets prior to Operation Storm in the area in the Republic of Serbian Krajina; that this -- evidence of this had been brought to General Gotovina's attention; that General Gotovina had denied that he was in control of the forces conducting that shelling, and in fact that was a lie, in fact he was in control of those forces. I want you to make that assumption and then tell me if those facts are true, would you then infer that -- well, would you use that as evidence to infer that his shelling in Knin was directed at civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would ask, Mr. President, for a foundation for that monologue that was just given. I know it's an assumption, but where does it -- where is it in the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I don't know whether you want to respond to that, to this specific question put by Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. President, that the Defence gave assumptions to the witness upon which he based his report. No foundation provided for those. These are hypotheticals to a witness. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's too easy, Mr. Russo, that the Defence just at random made suggestions to the witness. You may not agree with some of them, and some may be well disputed and not solid in your view, but the mere fact that -- just to state that there's no basis for those assumptions would -- by the way, would make the whole testimony totally useless. Let me try to rephrase your question and see what answer the witness gives us. If a commander would have a well-established reputation of always targeting civilian population, would that be an element when you would have to make any inferences from an attack if the civilian population was at least hit, to whatever extent, to that attack. May I suggest to you the following. May I suggest that I give an answer, and you would say whether it's right or not. Would the answer be, That would be an element in assessing that new event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take a look at question 1 in your addendum. That appears at page 23 of your report. Now, first, Professor, I note that embedded within the question put to you are several facts that already suggest the legitimacy of the shelling, and I'll ask you if you gray with me. For example, the question presupposes that the artillery was directed against military objectives in Knin, and you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that if the objective -- well, if the artillery was directed at anything other than the military objectives --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Per se violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. The question also -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I interrupted. But it's fairly -- it's not fairly -- it's manifestly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. The question also has embedded in it the presumption that the artillery attack was conducted in support of the infantry assault.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you would agree that even if some of the artillery was used not as a support of the infantry assault, but in fact as a means to get the civilians out of the town, you would agree that that would be unlawful; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you used that weapon system to deliberately terrorise the civilian population, it is an illicit use, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the unlawfulness of that use -- of that assumed use that I'm suggesting to you, to get the civilians out, it doesn't change, does it, if in addition to shelling to get the civilians out you also shell legitimate military targets and front-line positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So your hypothetical is that there's evidence that there are three deliberate objects of attack, command -- military objectives within the populated area, enemy front-line defensive positions, and non-military objectives within the populated area?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the deliberate attack of non-military objectives is a per se violation, irrespective of whether you're also attacking other lawful military objectives, if that's established.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course your answer to question 1 is entirely dependent, not only on the facts and assumptions provided to you but on the facts embedded in the question itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire addendum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you have now asked the witness to assume that some of the facts would be quite different, and then he very quickly answered "per se violation." If it was not -- now, therefore, from that it follows already that this witness, when answering this question, answered it in accordance with the facts implied in the question. If they would be different, the answer could still be the same; but if they would be different, the answer could also be different. So therefore, it seems so obvious to me that this is the case that I wonder what the reason is that you still want to verify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, what I was seeking to verify was whether the Professor's answer to question 1 depended on any information he received other than the information which is apparent to us from the face of the question and the facts and assumptions provided. The witness has indicated that he was orally briefed about the strategic and operational situation. I wanted to make sure that to the extent he's relying on anything in that conversation that we don't know about, we're informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should not have intervened. The situation has not become any clearer. It's not only less obvious to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did you want me to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I think on my first day of testimony, I don't think this opinion would have any merit whatsoever if it was disconnected from the operational concept to which these targets were associated. So that's why that briefing, I think, has to -- the general concept of the operation has to inform my assessment of an opinion. If I didn't know that General Gotovina was seeking to breach improved defensive positions by forces that were under the command and control of the individuals in these headquarters, then I don't know how I could make a rational assessment. I could say it's a military objective, but the real issue here is proportionality. And I don't think that Colonel Konings did anything different, to be candid with the Tribunal. I mean, I think he has to have had the broader context of the operation in mind when he renders an opinion on the propriety of attacking certain military objectives. So in that regard, other than these facts and assumptions, that's what was in the back of my mind, the general context of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you know that Brigadier Rajcic, General Gotovina's chief of artillery, testified that using 122-millimetre MBRL's on Milan Martic's residence would have violated the rule of distinction and the principle of proportionality; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I recall that off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'll refer the Court and counsel to transcript page 16592, lines 5 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, when I asked Brigadier Rajcic whether there would be any problem using 122-millimetre rockets at Martic's building, he answered: "Yes, because of the rule of distinction." He further explained: "When one analyses the use of multiple rocket-launchers which has a greater density of projectiles in terms of their impact on the target point, it covers a broader area with these rockets. If you compare it with the 130-millimetre cannon and the assessment was that the proportionality or the balance between what might happen to the buildings around the target was unacceptable." Now, I take it that you don't disagree with Brigadier Rajcic's assessment in that regard, do you?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First off, that may very well have been his assessment, but I don't think there's a categorical equation. You're talking about, and I'm confident the Tribunal knows this, a fact-intensive analysis. It's an anticipatory analysis that is clear from Article 51 of AP I; it's clear from the commentary; it's clear from the "travaux preparatoires"; and I believe even jurisprudence of this Tribunal has confirmed that. Based on all the facts and circumstances, the METT-T-C, the commander has to make an assessment: Will the collateral damage or incidental injury anticipated by his attack be excessive in relation to the anticipated concrete and direct military advantage? Now, if the general or his artillery officer made the judgement that the risk to the civilian population was excessive in relation to the anticipated value of using that weapon system against that target, that's their -- that's what their job is, to make that assessment. I would need to know, in my view to say that's absolutely right or that's questionable, every other element of the decision-making process. Why did they want to target him? What did they seek -- what effect did they seek to achieve by targeting him? What was the probability that that weapon system would achieve that effect? What was the situation of the civilian population in the area? What was the risk associated with the alternate means available? What alternate means were available? What risk would be associated with foregoing the attack? Now, I presume that that's what they did, or that's what the witness is referring to, and he comes to that conclusion. I think that's a reasonable conclusion. But if I change the facts and circumstances, I think I could create a hypothetical where the use of that weapon system could be determined to be lawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, what I was seeking was based on everything you've been told to assume and everything you were otherwise educated on about the case, whether you in fact disagree with that assessment, or whether you simply can't make an assessment if it was correct or not.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess my point is I'm not saying I think the assessment was erroneous. I think it was a legitimate assessment. I don't know if I have enough fact to know whether or not an alternate assessment would have been improper. But I assume it would have been because that was the -- if that was the assessment that was made, I assume it's predicated on that METT-T-C analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, when Brigadier Rajcic testifies that using MBRLs against Martic's building would be a problem because of the rule of distinction, what does that indicate to you about the use of that weaponry in that area?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It suggests to me that the brigadier believes that the use of that rocket system is improper in that area because of the inability to have any degree of pin-point accuracy to the effect. Now, this obviously, as you know, was addressed by Colonel Konings in his report and his addendum, where he asserted that the use of multiple-launch rockets in a populated area - and I'm paraphrasing - is per se unlawful because of your inability to control the effects. I responded to that in my report. I don't think there is a per se prohibition. I'm not suggesting it's a favoured method of warfare in a populated area. But there are very few per se prohibitions on weapon systems, and most of them take the form of specific treaties or protocols where the international community has made a judgement that under no circumstance could the use of this method or means of warfare be justified. If you create a hypothetical where there is an area-denial objective or an area-effects objective, where the collateral effects of the rocket might, in fact, be less harmful or present less risk for the civilian population, then you could have a situation where the use was lawful. So, as I say, I presume from that testimony that -- that his judgement was that the value of using that system was offset by the excessive risk. But it implicates this question of whether it is per se unlawful to use this system in an area with a known civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, the answer that I read to you of the brigadier's testimony didn't just indicate proportionality as a concern; it also indicated distinction. Those are two distinct considerations, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I think if you look at Article 51 of AP I, a disproportionate attack is one of three methods of defining an indiscriminate attack. An indiscriminate attack is prohibited because it violates the principle of distinction, and there are several ways that an attack can fall into the definition of indiscriminate. Violating the proportionality rule is one of a number of ways an attack can be indiscriminate. Using a weapons system that is incapable of distinguishing between a lawful object of attack and protected individuals is another definition of indiscriminate. My view, and I think this is clear from my report, is that the proportionality rule is indelibly linked to the principle of distinction, but I believe that what that quote you read to me reveals is an underlying assumption that the weapons system itself is per se indiscriminate in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, you foreshadowed me a bit, Professor, with respect to Article 51. The -- Article 51(4), subsection (c) is, I believe, the rule that you've just referred to, using a method or means of attack that is of a nature to strike military and civilian objects without distinction; right? And what I was asking you was whether Brigadier Rajcic's testimony, that using MBRLs to fire at Martic's building would violate the rule of distinction, did you understand that to mean that using MBRLs would run afoul of that particular provision of Article 51(4)?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to interpret what I believe the witness believed when he made that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes. Given the fact that he identified both distinction and proportionality, I'm asking you what you took that testimony to mean.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I -- my understanding -- or my reaction to that testimony is that -- there's a -- that they've both been conflated in his mind. The weapon is improper for use against this target because it -- it will produce an indiscriminate result. Now, that, as I said, I think presupposes an assumption that the value of using the weapon in this context is outweighed by the risk of excessive collateral damage or incidental injury. But there's also a flavour in the testimony that the nature of the weapon itself is improper for use in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how to interpret the "flavour" part. First of all, what's your basis for believing that the concepts of proportionality and distinction have been conflated in Brigadier Rajcic's mind?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you read it again to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
