utterances.text: Sure. I asked him whether there would have been a problem firing 122-millimetre rockets at Martic's building. He answered: "Yes, because of the rule of distinction ..." And then he said: "When one analyses the use of multiple ... rocket-launchers, which has a greater density of projectiles, in terms of their impact on the target point, it covers a broader area with these rockets if you compare it with the 130-millimetre cannon, and the assessment was that the proportionality or the balance between what might happen to the buildings around the target was unacceptable."

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basis for that is he's focussing on -- he emphasises the area effect of the weapon and compares it with a weapon system that he assumes or is implied from his testimony is more precise in terms of its ability to be controlled. So that leads me to think that - and again, I'm trying to read his mind through this statement, that he's thinking of two equations: Is this a weapons system that because of its area effect is, itself, improperly used in a populated area; and what are we trying to achieve with its use; and as a result of this area effect, is that objective legitimate to be sought by this weapons system? And I think both of them are proper considerations in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And Brigadier Rajcic's assessment in this regard, doesn't it indicate to you that Martic's building was, in fact, in a civilian populated neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think even the facts and assumptions said that he was in a building where there was civilians, I believe, perhaps I'm mistaken. Or he was in an apartment building. I -- my answer is I didn't -- I don't think I needed that to make that an element of my thought process. I assumed that Martic was in a building -- in an apartment building, which infers to me it's not a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well -- okay, I think -- I think I understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "A flat of Milan Martic was on the top floor of a multi-storey building that was built to house civilian police personnel." So maybe I was over presumptive there, but my assumption was it's a flat in an apartment that has civilians in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you did understand from Brigadier Rajcic's testimony that it was Milan Martic himself that was the target of the artillery attack and not the building; right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect that they sought to achieve was to kill or disrupt Milan Martic, yes. That was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll be moving on to another topic. I don't know if this is a proper time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it also depends on how much time you'd still need, Mr. Russo. And you -- well, you didn't promise, but you indicated you would tell us at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand we have double session tomorrow, Mr. President, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although it may be that we can start only a bit later in the afternoon, but let's -- you can -- yes. By the way, you're doing it the wrong way, Mr. Russo. Telling us how much time you need after you've asked how much time we have is the wrong order of thinking. Let me say that we have no afternoon session. Could you please give me your answer. Today we are assuming a lot of things. Let's assume that you have -- we have no afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, if we had no afternoon session, Mr. President, I think I would take the entire morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The entire morning session. Could I hear from the Defence how much time they would think they would need for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, very, very brief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very brief. I'm looking at the other Defence teams who will remain silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same for you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Russo, if we would have an afternoon session?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will certainly endeavour to complete the examination within the morning session. I understand the Court's concerns. If I had the rest of my examination to do, I would take both the morning and the afternoon's sessions. I am going to take the Court's guidance into consideration, cut my examination down significantly, and I will do my best to complete my examination in the morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is inclined, Mr. Russo, to allow you to use the morning session and not to immediately stop you if you were to use some of the first afternoon session. But before we'll give in to this inclination, I would like to know whether that would still remain within -- because the Chamber would like to finish the testimony of this witness tomorrow. And, Mr. Kehoe, that would not cause a problem to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will adjourn for the day. Yes, perhaps we could use the time for another matter which is still on my agenda. But, Professor Corn, you don't have to be bothered with what is still on our agenda. Assuming that tomorrow would be the 11th of September, we'd then resume on the 11th of September, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I. And I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, similar as I did before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would like to see you back tomorrow morning, and you know that there's a fair chance that we would not finish in the morning session, which would mean that more likely it will be 4.00, 5.00, or even 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate trying to get it completed tomorrow to accommodate my class schedule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the only reason why, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if that is a collateral effect of this decision, then it's not bad. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to deliver its decision on the expert report of Renaud de la Brosse. On the 22nd of July, 2009, the Gotovina Defence requested the Chamber to take judicial notice of the witness's expert report. On the 24th of July, 2009, the Chamber asked the Gotovina Defence to submit the report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, instead. This can be found at transcript pages 20710 and 711. And on the same day, the Gotovina Defence submitted the expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis. The Gotovina Defence submitted that the report relates to Counts 1, 2, and 3 of the indictment. The report concerns the use of propaganda by the Serbian authorities through the media and was previously admitted in the case of Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic. On the 18th of August, 2009, the Prosecution filed its notice, requesting the Chamber not to admit that report. The Prosecution contended that the report is not sufficiently relevant because it draws no connection between the use of propaganda and the departure of Serbs from Sector South. Moreover, the Prosecution submitted that the existence of Serbian propaganda is a background, non-contentious issue in this case and the report adds nothing significant to the material already in evidence. The Prosecution further indicated that should the Chamber decide to admit the report, it did not wish to cross-examine the witness. The general standards of admissibility set forth in Rule 89 of the Rules also apply to expert reports. Rule 89(C) provides that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. In addition, the Tribunal's jurisprudence sets out the following two requirements: First, for a proposed expert report to be probative, the witness who drafted the report must be considered an expert by the Chamber; and second, the content of the expert report must fall within the accepted expertise of the expert witness. An expert is a person who, by virtue of some specialised knowledge, skill, or training, can assist the trier of fact to understand or determine an issue in dispute. The Chamber notes that the expert status of the witness as such is not disputed by the parties. On the basis of the witness's curriculum vitae submitted on the 6th of May, 2003, by the Prosecution in the case of Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic, the Chamber is satisfied that the witness qualifies as an expert in the use of propaganda through the media and that the report falls within his expertise. The Chamber further notes that the report provides at least the required minimum degree of transparency in the sources and methods used. For these reasons, the Chamber is satisfied that the report is probative. With regard to relevance, the Chamber notes that the report discusses the control exercised by Serbian authorities over the Serbian media and the use of propaganda by Serbian authorities in order to further their political goals, by encouraging among Serbs fear and hatred of non-Serbs. It contains specific accounts of Serbian media reports from 1991 through 1993, alleging crimes committed by Croats against Serbs. The report further describes the depiction by the Serbian media in the same period of the Croatian community in general and the purported aims of the Croatian regime under President Tudjman specifically. The report does not address whether and to what extent civilians in Sector South were exposed to Serbian propaganda, nor does it make a connection between such propaganda and the departure of Serb civilians from Sector South. Nonetheless, the Chamber considers that the expert's discussion of propaganda in the Serbian media may assist the Chamber in understanding the information that may have been available to the Serb civilians leaving the Sector South area around the time of Operation Storm. As a result, the matter addressed in the report is relevant to the indictment, and in particular to the alleged charges of persecution of Count 1 and deportation and forcible transfer of Counts 2 and 3. For these reasons, the Chamber is satisfied that the report meets the requirements for admission set out in Rule 89(C) of the Rules as well as those set out in the Tribunal's jurisprudence, and admits the expert report of Witness de la Brosse into evidence. The Chamber instructs the Registrar to assign an exhibit number to the report and to inform the parties and the Chamber of the exhibit number so assigned. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the admission into evidence of the expert report of Witness de la Brosse.
